1.pericope_label: Learn not the way of the heathen; be not dismayed at the signs of heaven
debates: Whom the warning is addressed to
How the particle introducing the last clause of the second verse should be taken
What the signs of heaven are
outliers: Calvin holds the first word of the second verse a copying error for a particle the prophet uses elsewhere
themes: Warning given before the exile that would test it
Astrology feared where prophecy was despised
Heathen custom stealing in insensibly
A homely theology treated as a safeguard against superstition

3.pericope_label: The customs of the people are vain: one cutteth a tree out of the forest
debates: Whether the word means customs, statutes or idols
Which prophet copied the other in these parallel passages
Why the argument turns from astrology to images
outliers: Ellicott judges this chapter the copy and the earlier prophet the original, while allowing that the verses may be an interpolation
themes: Religious institutions distinguished from ordinary custom
A reputation for wisdom disabling judgement
Craftsmanship narrated as its own refutation
An image fastened so that it cannot move

5.pericope_label: Upright as the palm tree, but speak not
debates: Whether the fifth verse compares the idol to a pillar or to a scarecrow
Whether the fastening is of the image or of its metal plating
Why the argument turns from idols to God at this point
outliers: Ellicott prefers a rendering that makes the idol a scarecrow in a garden of gourds, against the received palm tree
themes: A figure that may be either stately or ridiculous
One prophet borrowing another to double the witness
The absurdity of a maker producing his own god
Idols only despicable once God is known

7.pericope_label: Who would not fear thee, O King of nations?
debates: Whether the title king of nations means acknowledged rule or rightful rule
Whether the wood is a doctrine of vanities or a rebuker of them
Whether all the heathen are brutish or brutish only in this one thing
outliers: Clarke reports a rendering that turns the wood from the subject of a false doctrine into a witness against it
themes: A question asked in indignation rather than inquiry
Universal sovereignty asserted against a national God
Wisdom that never arrived at its own object
A god assembled entirely from purchased materials

9.pericope_label: Silver spread into plates is brought from Tarshish
debates: Which country the first name denotes
Whether the second name is a place or a quality of the gold
Why the splendour of the idols is described at such length
outliers: Calvin places the first name in Cilicia where Ellicott and Clarke both place it in Spain
themes: A god whose parts are imported
Splendour granted in order to be dismissed
Three titles set against a manufactured thing
Truth named as the first attribute of the living God

11.pericope_label: The gods that have not made the heavens shall perish
debates: Whether the Aramaic verse is original or an interpolated gloss
Why the answer is given in the language of the conquerors
Whether the participles of the twelfth verse continue the preceding list
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch argue that no copyist would have interpolated a Chaldee verse into a Hebrew text, against several scholars who delete it
themes: One verse in a foreign tongue in the middle of a book
A confession put into the mouths of slaves
A wordplay preserved only in the original
Creation urged as the decisive difference

13.pericope_label: When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters
debates: Whether the disputed noun means multitude or sound
Whether the verse quotes a psalm or the psalm quotes it
Whether the idols mock their worshippers or are themselves mocked
outliers: Ellicott declines to say which of two verbally identical passages is the older, allowing that both may derive from a common source
themes: Change in nature set beside its fixed order
Natural explanation held not to exclude divine power
A thunderstorm as the clearest evidence of government
The maker shamed by what he has made

15.pericope_label: The portion of Jacob is not like them
debates: Whether the disputed word means mockery or delusion
Whether the threat falls on the idols or their makers
What the title portion of Jacob is drawn from
outliers: Calvin denies the sense of mockery that Ellicott and several versions give the word, deriving it instead from a verb meaning to lead astray
themes: Emptiness charged after falsehood
A judgment extended from the images to the men
Nations allotted gods and one people allotted God
Maker and made distinguished as the whole difference

17.pericope_label: Gather up thy wares out of the land, O inhabitant of the fortress
debates: Whether the seventeenth verse is addressed to Israel or to the Chaldeans
Whether the word means wares, a bundle or a travelling mantle
What the figure of the sling conveys
outliers: Calvin objects that the rabbinic reading takes the first verse of the Chaldeans while giving the second to Israel, though the two are connected
themes: A parenthesis closed and the threat resumed
Security mistaken for strength
Possessions reduced to what one hand can carry
Removal made thorough where it had been partial

19.pericope_label: Woe is me for my hurt; my tabernacle is spoiled
debates: Who is speaking from the nineteenth verse onward
Whether the tent stands for the city, the land or the people
Whether the metaphor is drawn from shepherds or from the church’s unsettled state
outliers: Calvin denies that the tent means the city, calling that reading strained and unsuitable
themes: A grief described as duty rather than as fact
Punishment accepted as the first step of reform
A city pictured as a collapsing tent
A people returned to the nomadic state they came from

21.pericope_label: The pastors are become brutish; a great commotion out of the north country
debates: How far the word shepherds extends
Whether the clause means they shall not prosper or they have not done wisely
What creature the last word of the twenty-second verse names
outliers: Clarke objects to the word bruit in the English version and cannot imagine how it got there
themes: Blame traced to those in authority without excusing the rest
Rank treated as exemption from reproof
A prediction confirmed by the enemy’s arrival
Cities left as a habitation for wild animals

23.pericope_label: O LORD, correct me, but with judgment, not in thine anger
debates: Whose way is meant in the twenty-third verse
Whether the psalm quoting these words borrowed from the prophet or the reverse
What asking for correction in measure concedes
outliers: Calvin infers from the limited request that the people could not ask outright pardon, having accumulated evils after many warnings
themes: Human purpose overruled at the point where roads divide
Chastisement accepted and only its degree contested
A difference asked between the punished and the ignorant
Two identical passages with no certain order of priority
